node.title: Organisms and Populations: Population attributes – birth and death rate, age pyramids;

questions.stem: The association of an alga and a fungus in a lichen is an example of
questions.explanation: In a lichen the fungus and the alga (or cyanobacterium) live together and both benefit. The alga makes food by photosynthesis, while the fungus gives protection and helps in absorbing water and minerals. A +/+ interaction in which both partners gain is called mutualism.

optionRationale.2: In commensalism only one species benefits and the other is unaffected, but here both gain.
optionRationale.3: In parasitism one species is harmed, which is not true of the lichen partners.
optionRationale.4: In amensalism one species is harmed and the other is unaffected.

questions.stem: The population density of a habitat increases because of
questions.explanation: Population density can change through four basic processes. Natality (births) and immigration (individuals coming in from outside) add individuals and raise the density, while mortality (deaths) and emigration (individuals leaving) remove individuals and lower it.

optionRationale.1: Emigration removes individuals from the habitat, so it lowers the density.
optionRationale.3: Mortality reduces the number of individuals.
optionRationale.4: Both mortality and emigration decrease the density.

questions.objective: State the factors that raise population density

questions.stem: The maximum number of individuals of a species that the resources of a habitat can support is its
questions.explanation: No habitat has unlimited resources. The limit on the number of individuals that the available food, space and other resources can sustain is the carrying capacity, usually written K. In logistic growth the population levels off at this value.

optionRationale.1: Biotic potential is the maximum reproductive capacity under ideal conditions, not the limit set by resources.
optionRationale.2: Birth rate is the number of births per unit time and is not a limit.
optionRationale.4: Population density is the number of individuals per unit area at a given time.

questions.stem: Plants such as Calotropis produce cardiac glycosides, which serve as
options: a store of nutrients for the seedling
questions.explanation: Plants cannot move away from grazers, so many have chemical defences. Calotropis produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides that make cattle and goats avoid it. Nicotine, caffeine, quinine and strychnine are other chemicals plants make to deter herbivory.

optionRationale.1: Pollinators are attracted by colour, scent and nectar, not by poisonous glycosides.
optionRationale.2: Seed dispersal is aided by fruit structures, not by glycosides.
optionRationale.3: Cardiac glycosides are toxins and are not a nutrient store.

questions.stem: Some zooplankton species in lakes and ponds survive adverse conditions by entering a stage of suspended development called
questions.explanation: Under unfavourable conditions many zooplankton species of lakes and ponds enter diapause, a stage of suspended development. Hibernation is winter sleep and aestivation is summer sleep of animals such as snails and fish, while migration is a temporary movement to another place.

optionRationale.1: Migration is the movement of the organism to a more hospitable area, not suspended development.
optionRationale.3: Aestivation is escape from summer heat or drought, shown by animals like snails and fish.
optionRationale.4: Hibernation is winter sleep of animals such as bears; the word used for zooplankton is diapause.

questions.objective: Identify diapause as a response to stress

questions.stem: Organisms that can tolerate a wide range of salinity are called
questions.explanation: Euryhaline organisms tolerate a wide range of salinity, whereas stenohaline organisms tolerate only a narrow range. The same prefixes apply to temperature, where eurythermal organisms tolerate a wide range and stenothermal organisms a narrow one.

optionRationale.1: Stenohaline organisms tolerate only a narrow range of salinity.
optionRationale.2: Stenothermal refers to a narrow temperature tolerance.
optionRationale.3: Eurythermal refers to a wide temperature tolerance, not salinity.

questions.objective: Use the terms eury- and steno- correctly

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about responses of organisms to the environment.
A. Regulators maintain a constant internal environment through physiological mechanisms.
B. In conformers the body temperature changes with the surrounding temperature.
C. Hibernation is winter sleep and aestivation is summer sleep.
D. Thermoregulation costs the body no energy.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Regulators keep the internal conditions constant (homeostasis) and conformers cannot, so their body temperature follows the surroundings, making A and B correct. Hibernation is winter sleep and aestivation is summer sleep, so C is correct. Thermoregulation uses a lot of energy, so D is wrong.

optionRationale.1: Statement C is also correct, so this is incomplete.
optionRationale.2: Statement A is also correct, so this is incomplete.
optionRationale.4: Statement D is false; maintaining a constant body temperature needs a large expenditure of energy.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on regulators, conformers and dormancy

questions.stem: Match List-I (organism or condition) with List-II (adaptation) and choose the correct code.

left: A. Kangaroo rat of the desert
right: I. Leaves reduced to spines and photosynthesis by the flattened stem
II. Oxidation of internal fat gives water and urine is concentrated
III. Increased production of red blood cells
IV. Basking in the sun when cold and burrowing when hot

questions.explanation: The kangaroo rat meets its water needs by oxidising internal fat and concentrates its urine (A-II). Opuntia has leaves reduced to spines, with the flattened stem doing photosynthesis (B-I). At high altitude the body makes more red blood cells (C-III), and desert lizards regulate temperature by behaviour, basking and burrowing (D-IV).

optionRationale.2: A and B are interchanged; spines belong to the cactus, not to the rat.
optionRationale.3: C and D are interchanged; basking and burrowing is lizard behaviour, and more red cells is the high-altitude response.
optionRationale.4: A and C are interchanged; more red blood cells is not an adaptation of the kangaroo rat.

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Parasites such as tapeworms have hooks and suckers.
Reason (R): Most parasites are host-specific.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Parasites such as tapeworms have adhesive organs like hooks and suckers to hold on to the host, and they are generally host-specific, so both statements are true. The hooks and suckers serve attachment, whereas host specificity is a separate adaptation, so R does not explain A.

optionRationale.1: Host specificity does not explain the presence of hooks and suckers, which are for attachment.
optionRationale.3: R is true; most parasites are adapted to a particular host.
optionRationale.4: A is true; tapeworms attach to the intestine with hooks and suckers.

questions.stem: A colony of 250 mice in a barn has 100 births and 40 deaths in a month. The per capita death rate per month is
questions.explanation: The per capita rate is the number of events divided by the number of individuals present. So the death rate is 40 / 250 = 0.16 per mouse per month. The figure 0.40 is the per capita birth rate (100 / 250), and the net gain of 60 mice gives a growth of 0.24 per capita.

optionRationale.1: 0.04 is not obtained from 40 divided by 250; this is a decimal error.
optionRationale.2: 0.40 is the birth rate, 100 / 250, not the death rate.

questions.objective: Calculate a per capita death rate

questions.stem: A population grows exponentially at $r = 0.05$ per day. Taking $\ln 2 = 0.693$, the time it takes to double is about
questions.explanation: For exponential growth $N_t = N_0 e^{rt}$. Doubling means $e^{rt} = 2$, so $t = \ln 2 / r = 0.693 / 0.05 = 13.86$, which is about 13.9 days. The doubling time does not depend on the starting population size.

optionRationale.1: 6.9 days results from using r = 0.1, not 0.05.
optionRationale.2: 27.7 days results from dividing by 0.025, which is half of r.
optionRationale.3: 3.5 days is the result for r = 0.2.

questions.objective: Calculate the doubling time of an exponential population

questions.stem: Which pair consists of organisms that both reproduce only once in their lifetime?
questions.explanation: Life history traits differ widely. Pacific salmon and bamboo reproduce only once in their lifetime, whereas most birds and mammals reproduce many times. A mango tree flowers every year, and oysters release large numbers of larvae repeatedly, so those are not once-only breeders.

optionRationale.2: Sparrows breed repeatedly in different seasons.
optionRationale.3: A mango tree flowers and fruits every year, so it breeds many times.
optionRationale.4: Oysters and elephants both breed more than once.

questions.objective: Identify organisms that breed once in a lifetime

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about population interactions.
A. Interspecific competition can occur even when resources are plentiful, if one species interferes with the feeding of the other.
B. Predators act as conduits for transferring energy fixed by plants to higher trophic levels.
C. The prickly pear cactus introduced into Australia was brought under control by a cactus-feeding moth.
D. An exotic species introduced into a new area never affects the native species.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Competition can reduce a species' feeding efficiency by interference even when resources are abundant (A). Predators pass energy to higher trophic levels (B), and the prickly pear in Australia was controlled by a cactus-feeding moth (C). Exotic species often affect natives badly, so D is false.

optionRationale.1: Statement C is also correct, so this misses it.
optionRationale.3: Statement D is false, and statement A is left out.
optionRationale.4: Statement D is false, and statement B is left out.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on competition and predation

questions.stem: A population of 400 has a per capita birth rate of 0.10 and a death rate of 0.04 each year, and there is no migration. If both rates stay constant, the population after two years is about
questions.explanation: The net per capita growth is 0.10 - 0.04 = 0.06 per year. After year one the population is 400 x 1.06 = 424. In the second year the growth applies to the new size, so it becomes 424 x 1.06 = 449.4, about 449.

optionRationale.1: 448 comes from adding 24 twice, which ignores that growth is applied to the larger population in the second year.
optionRationale.2: 424 is the population after only one year.
optionRationale.4: 464 would need a net growth of 0.16 over two years in a straight line, which is not the net rate.

questions.objective: Project population size from birth and death rates

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Mammals living in colder climates generally have shorter ears and limbs than related mammals in warmer climates (Allen's rule).
Reason (R): Shorter extremities reduce the surface area of the body and so minimise heat loss.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Allen's rule states that mammals of colder climates tend to have shorter ears and limbs. Smaller extremities expose less surface area to the cold, so less body heat is lost to the surroundings. R therefore gives the adaptive reason for the pattern in A.

optionRationale.2: R is the direct adaptive explanation of the rule in A, not an unrelated fact.
optionRationale.3: R is true; a smaller surface area means less heat loss.
optionRationale.4: A is true; Allen's rule describes exactly this pattern.
